# A000364: Euler (or secant or "Zig") numbers: e.g.f. (even powers only) sec(x) = 1/cos(x).

<!-- Generated by MathResearchLab. This file is rewritten on every sync; edit the app, not this file. -->

**Status:** Open per source; openness not yet verified

## Statement

Original wording (verbatim from the source):

```latex
Conjecture: taking the sequence [a(n) : n >= 1] modulo an integer k gives a purely periodic sequence with period dividing phi(k). For example, the sequence taken modulo 21 begins [1, 5, 19, 20, 16, 2, 1, 5, 19, 20, 16, 2, 1, 5, 19, 20, 16, 2, 1, 5, 19, ...] with an apparent period of 6 = phi(21)/2. · Peter Bala's conjectured congruences, a(2n) == 5 (mod 60) for n >= 1 and a(2n + 1) == 1 (mod 60), hold due to the results of Stern (mod 4) and Knuth & Buckholtz (mod 3 and 5).

Lean (formal-conjectures):
theorem main :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → ∃ p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ p ∣ k.totient ∧
      ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → Int.ModEq k (secantNumber (n + p)) (secantNumber n)
```

Normalized:

Conjecture: taking the sequence [a(n) : n >= 1] modulo an integer k gives a purely periodic sequence with period dividing phi(k). For example, the sequence taken modulo 21 begins [1, 5, 19, 20, 16, 2, 1, 5, 19, 20, 16, 2, 1, 5, 19, 20, 16, 2, 1, 5, 19, ...] with an apparent period of 6 = phi(21)/2. · Peter Bala's conjectured congruences, a(2n) == 5 (mod 60) for n >= 1 and a(2n + 1) == 1 (mod 60), hold due to the results of Stern (mod 4) and Knuth & Buckholtz (mod 3 and 5).

## Novelty pre-check

Verdict: **likely_open**. The statement says the two modulo-60 congruences “hold due to the results of Stern (mod 4) and Knuth & Buckholtz (mod 3 and 5).” That settles the modulo-60 case. R5 and R7 concern powers of two. No supplied record settles whether every positive modulus k admits a period dividing φ(k) starting at n = 1. This absence of evidence does not prove openness.
